description: We’re a team passionate about space, technology and storytelling. We want to transform NASA’s forgotten equipment on the Moon and Mars into stories that inspire curiosity and bring space history to life. If you’re creative, curious and excited about space, join us! We’re looking for people with skills in design, storytelling, 3D visualization, animation or development to build something truly out of this world.
summary:
ECHOES: The Stories We Left Behind is an interactive digital museum where NASA hardware left on the Moon and Mars tells its own story. Players explore the surface of each world, discover hidden equipment such as Opportunity, Ingenuity, Viking 1, the Apollo 11 site and Surveyor 3 and open an archive for each one.

Every object can be viewed in two modes built on the same data. Science Mode gives mission facts, instruments, dates and discoveries. Story Mode turns those facts into first-person narration, with every line clearly separated from verified fact. A scrubbable timeline walks through launch, arrival, science and the final signal, ending in a “SIGNAL LOST” sequence and real NASA imagery of where the hardware rests today. Quizzes and layered explanations (Beginner, Curious, Technical) reinforce learning.

ECHOES directly answers the challenge by telling each machine’s mission, science, journey and legacy for school-age learners. It matters because these machines inspired generations and their discoveries still shape future exploration. Built from official NASA sources, it makes that legacy memorable.
details:
What it does and how it works

ECHOES is an interactive web museum where NASA hardware left on the Moon and Mars tells its own story. Users choose a world, scan the surface, and discover hidden equipment such as Opportunity, Ingenuity, Viking 1, the Apollo 11 site and Surveyor 3. Each object has an archive with its mission, a scrubbable timeline from launch to final signal, the science it made possible, a “SIGNAL LOST” sequence, a “Where is it now?” section with real imagery, and a short quiz.

Every object can be viewed in two modes built from the same data. Science Mode shows facts, instruments, dates and discoveries. Story Mode retells those same events in first person. Each story line is tagged as fact or narration and linked to a NASA source, so the narration never adds events or science.

Benefits and intended impact

Young learners get an emotional way into NASA mission history, with explanations at Beginner, Curious and Technical levels. Source links and image credits show students where facts come from, which builds fact-checking habits. We want students to see that these missions’ legacies still shape how we explore the Moon and Mars.

Tools and technology

React, Tailwind CSS and Framer Motion, with static JSON data, deployed on Vercel. Data and imagery come from the NASA Image and Video Library API, NASA Open APIs (Mars Rover Photos manifest), LRO/LROC orbital imagery and NASA mission pages.

What makes it creative

  • Machines “speak,” but only through narration based on the mission record.
  • One timeline drives the whole story. As users drag it, the signal meter and the narration change, ending in a cinematic SIGNAL LOST moment followed by “But the science remains.”
  • A discovery mechanic (“UNKNOWN OBJECT DETECTED”) makes exploring feel like archaeology, not browsing a list.
  • Zooming into real orbital imagery shows that the hardware is still physically there.

What we considered

  • Accuracy first. The narration cannot add science, and the fact/narration tags make this visible in the interface. Mars durations use sols (Martian days), not Earth days.
  • Official sources only. Facts are hand-curated from NASA pages and linked to their source, with no random scraping.
  • A realistic scope. We focused on the Moon and Mars, as the challenge title says, and chose a small set of strong stories.
  • Accessibility and age range. We used readable type, strong contrast, simple interactions and layered explanations.
  • Reliability. Images and data are cached locally so the demo works even if an API is slow.
